bug_description.normalized: The fuzzer makes `test_face()` copy a non-empty glyph name into local `char buf[5]` and immediately call `hb_font_get_glyph_from_name(font, buf, strlen(buf), &g)`. Inside `OT::post::accelerator_t::get_glyph_from_name()`, local `hb_bytes_t st(name, len)` is passed to `hb_bsearch_r(&st, ...)`, but `hb_bytes_t` inherits `hb_array_t::operator&()` that returns `arrayZ`. The search key therefore becomes raw `buf`, `cmp_key()` casts that 5-byte stack buffer to `hb_bytes_t*`, and `hb_array_t<char const>::cmp()` reads the forged `len` field 8 bytes into the redzone, causing the observed stack-buffer-overflow read.

source.description: The glyph-name query fills `test_face`'s local `buf[5]` from the attacker-controlled face; that stack buffer is later reused as the reverse-lookup key.
source.value_from: The staged witness `poc` is exactly 32 bytes. In `test/fuzzing/hb-shape-fuzzer.cc`, `len` therefore becomes 32, and `memcpy(text32, data + size - len, len)` overwrites only the first 32 bytes of zero-initialized `uint32_t text32[16]`, leaving the last word `text32[15] == 0`; `test_face(face, text32[15])` therefore queries glyph 0 on this witness. The recorded crash proves this call produced a non-empty NUL-terminated name in `buf`, because line 62 reached `strlen(buf)` and `get_glyph_from_name()` instead of returning on `!len`.
source.note: This call asks HarfBuzz to materialize the queried glyph name into the local 5-byte stack buffer `buf`; on the witnessed path the next line reuses that same populated buffer as the vulnerable search key.

tainted_value_origin.description: The vulnerability-relevant key becomes the local stack buffer pointer `buf` plus its positive `strlen(buf)` result; those values feed local `hb_bytes_t st` inside `get_glyph_from_name()`.

root_cause.code: const uint16_t *gid = (const uint16_t *) hb_bsearch_r (&st, gids, count, sizeof (gids[0]), cmp_key, (void *) this);
root_cause.description: The code passes `&st` as the binary-search key even though `hb_bytes_t` inherits `hb_array_t::operator&()`, so the expression yields `st.arrayZ` (the raw `char*` name buffer) instead of the address of `st`.
root_cause.note: The fix changes only this call site: it adds `hb_addressof()` and passes `hb_addressof (st)` so `cmp_key()` receives a real `hb_bytes_t*` rather than the caller's stack buffer.

sink.description: ASAN crash site. The comparator reads the `len` field from a forged `hb_bytes_t` overlay on `test_face`'s `buf[5]`, so the 4-byte field load lands past the end of that stack object.
sink.note: ASAN reports a 4-byte stack-buffer-overflow read at offset 88 in `test_face`, while `buf` occupies `[80,85)`; `hb_array_t` stores `len` 8 bytes after `arrayZ`, matching a read from `buf + 8`.

parser_admitted.description: By this dispatch the input blob has already been accepted as a face and execution has entered `post`-table glyph-name handling, the subsystem that later performs the failing reverse lookup.

coarse_trace.summary: The fuzzer-driven face is queried for a glyph name, which populates local `buf[5]`, and that same stack buffer is immediately reused as the reverse-lookup key.
The reverse lookup wraps `buf` and `strlen(buf)` in local `hb_bytes_t st` and incorrectly passes `&st` to `hb_bsearch_r`.
Binary search forwards that raw key pointer into the comparator without repairing the type mismatch.
The comparator casts the raw `buf` pointer to `hb_bytes_t*` and dereferences it as the search key.
Reading the forged `len` field overreads 4 bytes past `buf[5]`, triggering the recorded stack-buffer-overflow.

fine_trace.note: This call asks HarfBuzz to materialize the queried glyph name into the local 5-byte stack buffer `buf`; on the witnessed path the next line reuses that same populated buffer as the vulnerable search key.

The same stack buffer is immediately reused as the reverse-lookup key: `name = buf` and `len = strlen(buf) > 0`, otherwise `get_glyph_from_name()` would stop at its `if (unlikely (!len)) return false;` check.
The lookup builds a local `hb_bytes_t` search-key object on the stack with `st.arrayZ = name` and `st.len = len`; here `name` still points to `test_face`'s `buf`.

fine_trace.code: const uint16_t *gid = (const uint16_t *) hb_bsearch_r (&st, gids, count, sizeof (gids[0]), cmp_key, (void *) this);
fine_trace.note: This call is the bug: `hb_bytes_t` is `hb_array_t<const char>`, and `hb_array_t::operator&()` returns `arrayZ` instead of the object's address. So `&st` evaluates to `st.arrayZ == name == buf`, not to `hb_bytes_t*`; the patch fixes this by calling `hb_addressof (st)`.

The comparator trusts `pk` to be a real `hb_bytes_t*` and reinterprets the raw pointer received from step 4. Because step 4 passed `buf`, this cast treats the 5-byte stack array as an `hb_bytes_t` object.
Dereferencing `*key` turns the bytes around `buf` into a forged `hb_bytes_t` comparison key and passes it to `hb_array_t<char const>::cmp()`.

The first field read from the forged key is its `len`. In `hb_array_t`, `len` sits 8 bytes after `arrayZ`, so with `pk == buf` this 4-byte read lands at `buf + 8`, outside `test_face`'s `[80,85) 'buf'` object and exactly matches ASAN's stack-buffer-overflow read of size 4.

format.name: 32-byte HarfBuzz font blob exercising the `post` glyph-name round trip in `hb-shape-fuzzer`
format.contract: The staged witness is the exact 32-byte blob `00 01 00 00 00 01 20 20 20 20 20 20 70 6f 73 74 20 20 20 20 00 00 00 00 20 20 20 20 20 20 20 20`. Because the file is only 32 bytes, `test/fuzzing/hb-shape-fuzzer.cc` leaves `text32[15] == 0`, so `test_face()` queries glyph 0. On the witnessed path the face state derived from that blob makes `hb_font_get_glyph_name(font, 0, buf, 5)` write a non-empty NUL-terminated glyph name into local `buf[5]`; the immediate `hb_font_get_glyph_from_name(font, buf, strlen(buf), &g)` call then reaches `hb_bsearch_r(&st, ...)`, where the overloaded address-of on `hb_bytes_t` turns the search key into raw `buf` and produces the recorded overread. This contract is limited to the staged witness and observed path, not all malformed fonts or all `post` tables.
